title: Buying a Home with VND 300 Million: 5 Ways to Use Leverage Safely
desc: Can VND 300 million buy a home? Bank loans, social housing, family funds, buying small then upgrading, or land to build gradually, with repayment examples.
summary: Five ways to use leverage when you have only about VND 300 million to buy a home, with monthly repayment examples and the risks to anticipate.
body: p

With about VND 300 million in hand, many young families wonder: wait a few more years, or borrow and buy now? “Leverage” means using borrowed money to own an asset larger than your own capital. Leverage helps you get a home sooner, but it also multiplies risk if your income is not enough to repay the debt. This article compares 5 common approaches, using assumed figures so that you can recalculate for your own circumstances.
h2
1. Before borrowing: determine your repayment capacity
p

A prudent rule: total monthly debt repayment (principal plus interest on all loans) should not exceed about 30-40% of the household's stable income, and you should still be able to keep a reserve fund. This is a reference threshold for safety, not a legal requirement; banks make their own assessments under their own criteria.
p

How to calculate equal monthly instalments is explained in detail in the article “How to calculate home loan instalments”. In this article, every example uses an assumed interest rate, not the rate of any specific bank.
h2
2. Option 1: a commercial bank loan
p

Assumed example: buying a VND 1.5 billion home with VND 300 million (20%) of your own money and borrowing VND 1.2 billion over 20 years, assuming a fixed interest rate of 10% per year, repaid in equal instalments:
ul
The monthly payment is about VND 11.58 million.
The total repaid after 20 years is about VND 2.78 billion, i.e. interest of nearly VND 1.58 billion.
Using the 30-40% threshold, the household needs a stable income of about VND 29-39 million per month.
p

When you borrow, the house is usually used as a mortgage: you keep and live in the house but use it to secure the loan (Article 317 of the Civil Code). If you cannot repay the debt when due, the asset may be enforced against (Article 299).
h2
3. Option 2: social housing - a preferential loan
p

If you belong to an eligible group and meet the conditions to buy social housing, you can borrow from the Vietnam Bank for Social Policies up to 80% of the contract value for a maximum term of 25 years (Clauses 3 and 5, Article 48 of Decree 100/2024/ND-CP), at an interest rate of 5.4% per year under Decree 261/2025/ND-CP.
p

Assumed example: a VND 1 billion social housing unit, borrowing VND 800 million over 25 years at 5.4% per year gives a payment of about VND 4.87 million per month. For the eligibility and income conditions, see Conditions for buying social housing.
h2
4. Option 3: pooling funds with family
p
Parents, brothers and sisters adding money reduces the bank loan. To avoid later disputes, put clear paperwork in place:
ul
If it is a loan: record the amount, term and interest (if any). An interest rate agreed between individuals may not exceed 20% per year (Article 468 of the Civil Code).

If you are co-owners on the title (co-ownership in shares): state each person's share clearly (Article 209). When one person wants to sell their share, the others have a priority right to buy it (Clause 3, Article 218).
h2
5. Options 4 and 5: buy small then upgrade, or buy land and build gradually
ul

Buy small first: for example, a VND 800 million unit with a VND 500 million loan over 20 years (assuming 10% per year) means about VND 4.83 million per month. The pressure is much lower; after a few years you can sell to buy a larger one (note the taxes and fees on sale; see personal income tax on selling property).

Buy land and build gradually: suitable where land is still affordable. You need to check the planning and building permit and budget the construction cost; a detailed comparison is in the article “Buying land to build a house or buying a ready-made house”.
h2
6. Three risks to anticipate
ol
Rising interest rates after the preferential period - test with a rate 2-3% per year higher to see whether you can still pay.
Falling income (job loss, illness) - you need a reserve fund of at least several months of loan repayments.
House prices not rising as expected - do not borrow on the assumption that “selling will be profitable”.
note

This article is for reference only and is not financial advice. The figures are examples using assumed interest rates; actual interest rates and loan conditions are decided by the bank. Consider your family's repayment capacity and ask the bank carefully before signing. The 5.4% per year rate follows Decree 261/2025/ND-CP; Decree 100/2024/ND-CP is partly expired and may have been amended by documents not yet in our library.
